1. md-washington-county-2026: county moratorium. Applies: yes. Reason: in effect on 2026-10-26 and site within scope. Computed effective 2026-06-30, expires 2026-12-29. Parameters: effective 2026-06-30, duration_days: 182, scope countywide, exempt_if_permits_submitted: false. Evidence includes multiple quotes. There's a conflict: the draft ordinance says six months, but the Moratorium Nation dataset says 12-month moratorium. The computed expiration uses 182 days (6 months). The dataset says 12-month moratorium. The evidence includes both. The rule applies yes. The exemption: "The definition of 'Data Center' and the deferral does not apply to any use currently permitted under the Zoning Ordinance and for which a current Certificate of Use & Occupancy was disseminated as of the effective date of this Ordinance." The project has permits_submitted: false, and it's a new 300 MW data center, so likely not exempt.

2. federal-title-v-major-source: applies yes. Reason: estimated NOx potential to emit 1,067 tpy meets the 100 tpy major-source threshold. For md-washington-county-2026: The moratorium is in effect as of 2026-10-26, expires 2026-12-29. It defers all data center applications countywide. The project has not submitted permits. The exemption only applies to uses with a current Certificate of Use & Occupancy as of effective date. This project is new, so not exempt. The moratorium blocks acceptance, processing, reviewing, and approval of all applications for data centers. This seems like a fatal block right now. However, the moratorium expires 2026-12-29 (about two months from as_of date). But the rule says "fatal: blocks the project now". Since the moratorium is currently in effect and the project cannot even submit applications, it's a fatal block now. But the project could wait until after the moratorium expires. However, the verdict is about current viability. The moratorium is a temporary deferral for six months. The project cannot proceed now. I'd grade this as fatal because it blocks the project now. But the moratorium is temporary; after it expires, the project could proceed. However, the rule is "fatal: blocks the project now". The moratorium does block now. So fatal.

For federal-title-v-major-source: The project would need a Title V operating permit because estimated NOx PTE exceeds 100 tpy. This is a major source threshold. Obtaining a Title V permit is costly and slow (major). It doesn't block the project entirely but adds significant time and cost. So grade major.

Now, the verdict: The project faces a county moratorium that currently blocks all data center applications (fatal) and would require a federal Title V permit (major). The moratorium is temporary but in effect now. The project cannot proceed until the moratorium lifts. So verdict could be "no-go" because the moratorium blocks now. However, "no-go" might imply permanently blocked. The moratorium expires in two months. The verdict options: go, conditional, no-go, needs_confirmation. "conditional" might mean it can go if conditions met. "needs_confirmation" means need more info. The moratorium is a clear block now. The Title V permit is a major hurdle but not a block. The moratorium is fatal. So verdict "no-go" because the project cannot proceed now due to moratorium. But the moratorium is temporary; after it expires, the project could apply. However, the verdict is as of 2026-10-26. The project cannot proceed now. So "no-go" seems appropriate.

The project's 300 MW load assumes N+1 backup design of 121 diesel generators at 2,500 kW each, yielding estimated NOx PTE 1,067 tpy, exceeding 100 tpy threshold, triggering Title V permit. The exemption for existing permitted uses with Certificate of Use & Occupancy does not apply to this new project. Therefore, the project cannot submit applications until the moratorium lifts, and even then would face a major federal air permit requirement.
